PRASA VANDALISM EXPOSED

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Opportunistic criminals are targeting PRASA train stations left non-operational during COVID-19 – stripping every piece of copper and steel they can carry away.

Unique Selling Point:
** FOOTAGE OF THIEVES IN THE ACT ON THE TRACKS
** CCTV OF THIEVES HITTING BUSINESSES
** UNDERCOVER INVESTIGATION
** OPPORTUNITY FOR CONFRONTS

Summary:
Last year we covered the big business behind cable theft exploring crime trends, syndicates and new legislation delivering harsh sentences for offenders.

This year desperation rules. Low level opportunistic thieves are busy carrying off PRASA train stations bit by bit. With LockDown public transport came to standstill. Criminals moved in stealing copper and steel in broad daylight.

We have footage of the thieves in action.

In this insert we explore the crime spike and explore the impacts.


Further information:
WHY DO WE CARE ABOUT CABLE THEFT? THE IMPACT IS SEVERE
Currently copper is sold for R100 per kg. It’s a good return for stolen goods by anyone’s standard. But it’s not just a piece of cable – the pillaging of train stations and rail infrastructure will cost the country millions if not billions to rebuild.

SEXY ELEMENTS
Footage of criminals stealing in middle of day. I’ve been down to the tracks on the east rand – and its incredible to see. While I was there three guys were stripping away and eventually walked of with a drain cover.

IMPACT ON SOCIETY
Over 672 000 daily train commuters have been left stranded by the collapse of train services across Gauteng.

Over the last three years, 1 833 incidents of train stations have been vandalised at a replacement cost in excess of R2-billion.
This meant 800 daily trips, 585 daily trips have been cancelled due to the vandalism, resulting in a staggering financial loss to Prasa of over R173-million per year. THIS HAS NOT BEEN EXARCERBATED BY LOCKDOWN AND EVEN LESS TRAINS RUNNING – OPENING THE DOOR TO THIEVES
Railway services are a vital artery for our economy and getting people to work and places of opportunity in what is supposed to be a safe and affordable mode of transport.
The type of vandalism includes that to both conventional and modern signalling system, signals and train detection cables, including battery banks at signalling equipment rooms, multiple spans of contact and catenary wire overhead track equipment (OHTE) and transformers, rectifiers and various components at substations.
Due to the vastly reduced number of train services, trains that are still operating have become overcrowded to such an extent it is now common cause to see commuters hanging from the sides of the train or even sitting on top of the train.
Hundreds of thousands of ordinary South Africans rely on affordable and reliable transportation to get to and from work and to seek work. By not having a reliable train service, people are being forced to use other modes of transport at an increased cost to their household budget.
SMALL BUSINESS IMPACT
Businesses along the non-operational tracks are being ransacked and stripped as well – I have CCTV footage of this.

CASE STUDY
A scrap dealer right next door to the Wadeville train station has seen the structure being carried away bit by bit each day in the last three months. He has a great grasp of the situation and the illegal market – kind of like an industry insider with a front row seat to the destruction.

UNDERCOVER ELEMENT
We send an operative to sell copper to one of the dodgy scrapdealers with a hidden camera – we can bust them afterwards. Might be worth going into two or three.

** WORKING ON THIS

WHAT IS PRASA DOING
NOTHING is the short answer. The allegation is that they cancelled all security at these stations during lockdown – making it easy pickings for thieves.

**WORKING ON GETTING PRASA INSIDER

PRICE THEFT HYPOTHESIS
Crime is influenced by economic factors. If the price of copper goes up so too will the number of cable theft incidents simply because there is more money to be made.

These criminals are clever - they know the system, they know the market.

KILL THE MARKET – KILL THE CRIME
These investigators are taking their investigation to the next level – they realise there is no point in arresting the cable cutter or runner – they need to get to syndicate and ensure they are put behind bars with unquestionable evidence if they are going to make a difference to this crime trend.

They use all their resources and attempt to take every case full circle. Catching the small guys just won’t cut it.

Script:


SCRIPT: PRASA VANDALISM

VO: Infrastructure vandalism for profit impacts on most sectors across South Africa - from telecommunications to electricity to transportation. It is not a new crime trend. But today, it is more rife than ever before.

LINK: The PRASA rail network has been one of the hardest hit with opportunistic criminals ripping out anything and everything they can carry. It's billions of rands in infrastructure damage happening every day in broad daylight.

VO: Watch as thieves rip up platforms with pick axes, strip ticket offices unphased by cameras and shamelessly walk off with drain covers. In the time of COVID-19, desperation seems to rule - leaving no piece of infrastructure immune to theft.

SEAN: //It doesn't stop. I've come to work at 7:00 in the morning and people are busy and it'll go right through.

VO: Business owner Sean Stanford has premises adjacent to the Wadeville train station in Johannesburg.

SEAN: // it's quite depressing our station has been totally carried away piece by piece. // there's no security around. // And that no one's at work // And it's a free for all as you can see.

LINK: This is unbelievable. It's shocking to think that four months ago this station was operational.

VO: Much of PRASA’s rail network has been left exposed for almost eight months after external security contracts were cancelled and guards around the country were withdrawn.

The decision to cancel contracts was prompted by the Public Protector’s 2015 Derailed report that found some of the contracts were irregularly awarded.

MGITYWA: there was a feeding frenzy you know money was just being looted.

VO: PRASA Spokesperson Makhosini Mgitywa claims that some of the other contracts were cancelled – not because they were irregular, but rather because they apparently weren’t delivering value.

MGITYWA: This is a problem when you're dealing with an institution which was consumed by malfeasance and corruption that people who were supposed to act in the best interests of process were acting in the best interests of security companies and themselves

VO: While four implicated PRASA employees were fired and some security operators are legally challenging the contract termination - the looting on the ground hasn’t stopped. LockDown brought passenger trains to a halt, giving low level thieves unlimited access to stations, platforms and rail networks.

HERMAN: It is almost like anarchy has been declared, war on. On the railway assets //.

VO: Railway Safety Expert Herman Bruwer has 45 years experience in railway operation, risk management and safety regulations - he is shocked by the level of sudden destruction.

HERMAN: // the future for passenger rail services are very bleak in South Africa. The devastation // as a direct result of vandalism and theft of off the railway assets render the service utterly useless //

LINK: It's incredible to see it's kilometres on kilometers of dug out trenches where copper cable has been stolen and when you look on the side all you'll find are these casings and that's all that's left.

VO: Black market copper will go through small informal smelting operations run by dodgy scrap dealers – the stolen material is smelted into unidentifiable blocks.

We took our investigation undercover.

LINK: So. We have. This wheely bin with a hidden camera. But. You're not supposed to see it because it's hideous. And inside you've put some. Legal. And some illegal scrap. It seems we get some takers

VO: While some refused to buy the dodgy scrap, two bucket shops were all too happy to take the loot - we were paid well below legitimate market prices - getting R15 a kg from the one and R25 at the other - and of course no questions asked about the origin of the material.

By law, record needs to be kept of the seller’s details in terms of the Secondhand Goods Act.

The undercover agent, says these buyers know the stuff is illegal.

AGENT: /they paid me and only asked me not to tell other people that they do buy it and I must be careful of the police when I am coming there

VO: The best way to catch the thieves is usually in the act. We accompanied a private security tactical response team in pursuit of some thieves that were spotted looting at Katlehong Station, south of Joburg.

Watch as one of the suspects is chased through the informal settlement and eventually taken down.

LINK: Two guys have been caught - many other running all over the place when we got to the station.

VO: The impact of this crime is far reaching - with more than 130 stations destroyed and only 15% of PRASA’s network currently operational. Paul Soto from the United Commuters Voice, says commuters are feeling the pressure.

PAUL: // It's going deep into pockets of the commuters that will no longer manage to go to work because of the money that his work is getting. It's going to a transport //

VO: A return train ticket from Vereeniging to Pretoria costs around R25, while a return taxi trip will cost R180. It’s simply unaffordable for many low income earners who now find themselves having to walk along on the tracks while the trains are not running.

MAC: HOW LONG TO FIX?
HERMAN: I would estimate to normalize that RAILway. And that is only the devastation caused by vandalism will at least take two years and a couple of billion rands. //M12

MAC: //Not having a contingency plan has led to this vandalism has led to the looting of these state assets and it's poor planning.
MGITYWA: There was a contingency plan contingency plan that didn't work as well as it could have.

VO: PRASA deployed limited internal security and called on the police for assistance, while attempting an emergency procurement process that Mgitywa claims was sabotaged. He points out that PRASA’s problems are systemic and run deep.

MGITYWA: there's a lot of rogue elements within supply chain management. PRASA is under administration. It's under administration because there was just a gridlock here.

VO: But in the meantime, this criminality continues relentlessly - with thieves targeting state assets across the country - stealing lifts, stripping transformers and cutting overhead electrification cables.

If successfully prosecuted, criminals found guilty of tampering, damaging or stealing essential infrastructure can get as much as 30 years direct imprisonment or a fine of up to R100 million.

And the thieves are fully aware of the risk. As we entered Benrose Yard, the roads were barricaded and spotters alerted the culprits who scattered in all directions.

LINK: In november last year, This was a fully functioning railway track. It's been stripped apart piece by piece.

VO: If you look carefully, you can see the stolen material stacked neatly at the edge of the informal settlement.

NICK: They’ve taken everything you can see the overhead lines have gone underground cable , sleepers they leave nothing.

VO: Team Leader Nick van Loggerenberg says the culprits come prepared - armed with tools and weapons.

MAC: How much is it even worth is it worth anything really.
NICK: Yeah it's worth it in the bulk that they doing it and the copper is really worth it.

LINK: Masses of illegal copper is making it into the industry undetected it gets smelted and reformed and then it's resold into the legitimate market usually for export at even higher prices.

VO: It’s estimated that roughly 250 containers of copper valued at around R600 million is allegedly exported to China and India – illegally - every month.

It was time to pay the dodgy scrap dealers we caught on camera a visit - first up a bucket shop located in Benoni.

MAC: Are you guys buying illegal copper here
NIGEL: i haven’t bought any illegal copper,

VO: That’s not true… here he is, paying the agent cash for illegal copper. He gave in and showed us where the illegal material was hidden.

MAC - this is illegal

VO: The worker claimed he was following his boss, Victor’s instructions.

OWNER: i dont buy those things
MAC: Yes you do… told Nigel when people come here he must hide it at the back
OWNER: I’m sorry //
MAC Don’t apologise Victor, stop what you are doing

VO: The second bucket shop is in Bredell. The owner and his worker kept denying that anything dodgy was bought and tried to show us legitimate scrap.

WORKER: it’s not copper this one is wire
MAC” we know that this wire where is the one that we sold to you today.

VO: When it sank in that we were onto them - they reluctantly took us to their illegal stash that was kept under lock and key at the back.

MAC - This is itWHY YOU taking THIS THING
WORKER I told him i cant buy this thing
MAC - baba - you cant buy - how? it is here by you, how did it get by you?
WORKER: That;s why …He said he want money for food and i give him...
MAC - so there is no copper here - let’s look.. no no no BABA! you are running an operation here!!

VO: The pile of stolen material, from a range of state owned entities is valued at around R20 000. The owner Babu eventually owned up.

MAC: all of this illegal stuff - police must arrest you for this….
OWNER: ok boss I’m SORRY

VO: In order to kill the crime, you need to eliminate the market - but first it seems the infrastructure needs to be protected.

PRASA now attempts to insource security by employing 3000 guards that will hopefully become operational next month.

MAC: Security guards that need to be trained. How long is that going to take.
MGITYWA: No we we are looking for people who do not need training Because we want people who are going to hit the ground running

VO: While Mgitywa is positive that consequence management will make the difference, Bruwer is sceptical about these operational changes.

HERMAN: There's there's not enough time to play catch up in your maintenance and in your repairs. I'm a firm believer that PRASA // is not in the security business. Their prime concern should be the transportation of freight and passengers

VO: It will take a multipronged approach not only using technology and skills, but it will also require society to change its attitude towards infrastructure damage, believes Mgitywa.

MGITYWA: And sometimes make the mistake of thinking because use trains we it doesn’t affect us. // the attack on PRASA infrastructure is an attack on the country is an attack. On the economy is an attack on poor people.// ….


PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO: We rig hidden cameras into a trolley bin for a special undercover investigation, revealing how opportunistic criminals feed an illict black market with material from vandalised railway stations.

PROMO 2
VO: We go undercover and bust a bucket shop on the East Rand buying illegal scrap metal.
MAC: You know this wrong – look at this you are running an operation here!!

PROMO 3
VO: An undercover investigation exposes relentless infrastructure vandalism and brazen looting where opportunistic criminals feed an illicit black market that costs the economy billions.

PAUL: // It's going deep into pockets of the commuters that will no longer manage to go to work because of the money that his work is getting. It's going to a transport // VO: A return train ticket from Vereeniging to Pretoria costs around R25, while a return taxi trip will cost R180. It’s simply unaffordable for many low income earners who now find themselves having to walk along on the tracks while the trains are not running. MAC: HOW LONG TO FIX? HERMAN: I would estimate to normalize that RAILway. And that is only the devastation caused by vandalism will at least take two years and a couple of billion rands. //M12 MAC: //Not having a contingency plan has led to this vandalism has led to the looting of these state assets and it's poor planning. MGITYWA: There was a contingency plan contingency plan that didn't work as well as it could have. VO: PRASA deployed limited internal security and called on the police for assistance, while attempting an emergency procurement process that Mgitywa claims was sabotaged. He points out that PRASA’s problems are systemic and run deep. MGITYWA: there's a lot of rogue elements within supply chain management. PRASA is under administration. It's under administration because there was just a gridlock here. VO: But in the meantime, this criminality continues relentlessly - with thieves targeting state assets across the country - stealing lifts, stripping transformers and cutting overhead electrification cables. If successfully prosecuted, criminals found guilty of tampering, damaging or stealing essential infrastructure can get as much as 30 years direct imprisonment or a fine of up to R100 million. And the thieves are fully aware of the risk. As we entered Benrose Yard, the roads were barricaded and spotters alerted the culprits who scattered in all directions. LINK: In november last year, This was a fully functioning railway track. It's been stripped apart piece by piece. VO: If you look carefully, you can see the stolen material stacked neatly at the edge of the informal settlement. NICK: They’ve taken everything you can see the overhead lines have gone underground cable , sleepers they leave nothing. VO: Team Leader Nick van Loggerenberg says the culprits come prepared - armed with tools and weapons. MAC: How much is it even worth is it worth anything really. NICK: Yeah it's worth it in the bulk that they doing it and the copper is really worth it. LINK: Masses of illegal copper is making it into the industry undetected it gets smelted and reformed and then it's resold into the legitimate market usually for export at even higher prices. VO: It’s estimated that roughly 250 containers of copper valued at around R600 million is allegedly exported to China and India – illegally - every month. It was time to pay the dodgy scrap dealers we caught on camera a visit - first up a bucket shop located in Benoni. MAC: Are you guys buying illegal copper here NIGEL: i haven’t bought any illegal copper, VO: That’s not true… here he is, paying the agent cash for illegal copper. He gave in and showed us where the illegal material was hidden. MAC - this is illegal VO: The worker claimed he was following his boss, Victor’s instructions. OWNER: i dont buy those things MAC: Yes you do… told Nigel when people come here he must hide it at the back OWNER: I’m sorry // MAC Don’t apologise Victor, stop what you are doing VO: The second bucket shop is in Bredell. The owner and his worker kept denying that anything dodgy was bought and tried to show us legitimate scrap. WORKER: it’s not copper this one is wire MAC” we know that this wire where is the one that we sold to you today. VO: When it sank in that we were onto them - they reluctantly took us to their illegal stash that was kept under lock and key at the back. MAC - This is itWHY YOU taking THIS THING WORKER I told him i cant buy this thing MAC - baba - you cant buy - how? it is here by you, how did it get by you? WORKER: That;s why …He said he want money for food and i give him... MAC - so there is no copper here - let’s look.. no no no BABA! you are running an operation here!! VO: The pile of stolen material, from a range of state owned entities is valued at around R20 000. The owner Babu eventually owned up. MAC: all of this illegal stuff - police must arrest you for this…. OWNER: ok boss I’m SORRY VO: In order to kill the crime, you need to eliminate the market - but first it seems the infrastructure needs to be protected. PRASA now attempts to insource security by employing 3000 guards that will hopefully become operational next month. MAC: Security guards that need to be trained. How long is that going to take. MGITYWA: No we we are looking for people who do not need training Because we want people who are going to hit the ground running VO: While Mgitywa is positive that consequence management will make the difference, Bruwer is sceptical about these operational changes. HERMAN: There's there's not enough time to play catch up in your maintenance and in your repairs. I'm a firm believer that PRASA // is not in the security business. Their prime concern should be the transportation of freight and passengers VO: It will take a multipronged approach not only using technology and skills, but it will also require society to change its attitude towards infrastructure damage, believes Mgitywa. MGITYWA: And sometimes make the mistake of thinking because use trains we it doesn’t affect us. // the attack on PRASA infrastructure is an attack on the country is an attack. On the economy is an attack on poor people.// …. PROMOS PROMO 1 VO: We rig hidden cameras into a trolley bin for a special undercover investigation, revealing how opportunistic criminals feed an illict black market with material from vandalised railway stations. PROMO 2 VO: We go undercover and bust a bucket shop on the East Rand buying illegal scrap metal. MAC: You know this wrong – look at this you are running an operation here!! PROMO 3 VO: An undercover investigation exposes relentless infrastructure vandalism and brazen looting where opportunistic criminals feed an illicit black market that costs the economy billions. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Opportunistic criminals are targeting PRASA train stations left non-operational during COVID-19 – stripping every piece of copper and steel they can carry away.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: ** FOOTAGE OF THIEVES IN THE ACT ON THE TRACKS ** CCTV OF THIEVES HITTING BUSINESSES ** UNDERCOVER INVESTIGATION ** OPPORTUNITY FOR CONFRONTS
metadata.Summary: Last year we covered the big business behind cable theft exploring crime trends, syndicates and new legislation delivering harsh sentences for offenders. This year desperation rules. Low level opportunistic thieves are busy carrying off PRASA train stations bit by bit. With LockDown public transport came to standstill. Criminals moved in stealing copper and steel in broad daylight. We have footage of the thieves in action. In this insert we explore the crime spike and explore the impacts.
metadata.Further information: WHY DO WE CARE ABOUT CABLE THEFT? THE IMPACT IS SEVERE Currently copper is sold for R100 per kg. It’s a good return for stolen goods by anyone’s standard. But it’s not just a piece of cable – the pillaging of train stations and rail infrastructure will cost the country millions if not billions to rebuild. SEXY ELEMENTS Footage of criminals stealing in middle of day. I’ve been down to the tracks on the east rand – and its incredible to see. While I was there three guys were stripping away and eventually walked of with a drain cover. IMPACT ON SOCIETY Over 672 000 daily train commuters have been left stranded by the collapse of train services across Gauteng. Over the last three years, 1 833 incidents of train stations have been vandalised at a replacement cost in excess of R2-billion. This meant 800 daily trips, 585 daily trips have been cancelled due to the vandalism, resulting in a staggering financial loss to Prasa of over R173-million per year. THIS HAS NOT BEEN EXARCERBATED BY LOCKDOWN AND EVEN LESS TRAINS RUNNING – OPENING THE DOOR TO THIEVES Railway services are a vital artery for our economy and getting people to work and places of opportunity in what is supposed to be a safe and affordable mode of transport. The type of vandalism includes that to both conventional and modern signalling system, signals and train detection cables, including battery banks at signalling equipment rooms, multiple spans of contact and catenary wire overhead track equipment (OHTE) and transformers, rectifiers and various components at substations. Due to the vastly reduced number of train services, trains that are still operating have become overcrowded to such an extent it is now common cause to see commuters hanging from the sides of the train or even sitting on top of the train. Hundreds of thousands of ordinary South Africans rely on affordable and reliable transportation to get to and from work and to seek work. By not having a reliable train service, people are being forced to use other modes of transport at an increased cost to their household budget. SMALL BUSINESS IMPACT Businesses along the non-operational tracks are being ransacked and stripped as well – I have CCTV footage of this. CASE STUDY A scrap dealer right next door to the Wadeville train station has seen the structure being carried away bit by bit each day in the last three months. He has a great grasp of the situation and the illegal market – kind of like an industry insider with a front row seat to the destruction. UNDERCOVER ELEMENT We send an operative to sell copper to one of the dodgy scrapdealers with a hidden camera – we can bust them afterwards. Might be worth going into two or three. ** WORKING ON THIS WHAT IS PRASA DOING NOTHING is the short answer. The allegation is that they cancelled all security at these stations during lockdown – making it easy pickings for thieves. **WORKING ON GETTING PRASA INSIDER PRICE THEFT HYPOTHESIS Crime is influenced by economic factors. If the price of copper goes up so too will the number of cable theft incidents simply because there is more money to be made. These criminals are clever - they know the system, they know the market. KILL THE MARKET – KILL THE CRIME These investigators are taking their investigation to the next level – they realise there is no point in arresting the cable cutter or runner – they need to get to syndicate and ensure they are put behind bars with unquestionable evidence if they are going to make a difference to this crime trend. They use all their resources and attempt to take every case full circle. Catching the small guys just won’t cut it.
